topic: The mere exposure effect: why you like what's familiar
title: Why You Like What You've Seen a Lot
voiceover: Why do you like what you've seen a lot? In 1968, Robert Zajonc proposed the mere exposure effect. Repeated exposure to something can make you like it more. Zajonc's claim was that mere repeated exposure, with nothing else added, enhances attitudes. His 1968 paper described four kinds of evidence, from word frequency to controlled exposure experiments. In 2017, Matthew Montoya and colleagues analyzed 268 curve estimates from 81 articles. Liking rose with repeated exposure, then leveled off and declined. So more exposure helps up to a point; overexposure can backfire. Their meta-analysis covered effects on liking, familiarity and recognition. So familiarity can make something feel better, but don't mistake 'I've seen it a lot' for 'it's good'. Tomorrow: why do you get déjà vu?

description: Does seeing something again and again make you like it more? Zajonc proposed the mere exposure effect in 1968, and a 2017 meta-analysis found liking rises with exposure and then levels off and declines. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2, Pt.2), 1-27. Source: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., Vevea, J. L., Citkowicz, M., & Lauber, E. A. (2017). A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking. Psychological Bulletin, 143(5), 459-498.
accuracy_note: Montoya et al. (2017) is a meta-analysis of 81 articles; shapes vary by stimulus and number of exposures. The video does not claim familiarity makes things objectively better.
